newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Working for professionalism in humanitarian aid.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Working for professionalism in humanitarian aid.

text.p: For Professor Debarati Guha-Sapir humanitarian aid is not just a question of pouring money and enthusiastic volunteers into Third World refugee camps.

The director of the world-famous Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters says millions of dollars and hard work can come to nothing if not professionally managed. A little common sense and imagination can work wonders.

When the Calcutta-born public-health expert is not training aid professionals on how to give value for money she can be working on techniques for minimising the effects of natural disasters from volcanos to earthquakes, hurricanes to floods.
But as the world's disasters move increasingly from the natural to the man-made more and more of her time is taken up finding ways of helping refugees caught in the crossfire of conflict.

That took her to Nepal recently to research the reproductive health needs of Tibetan refugee women. On the eve of the visit she told Reuters that aid would already be more effective if only the international community would recognise a simple fact:
"Women and children altogether have generally been identified as representing about 80 percent of refugee populations," she said from an office covered with maps of world disasters.

"Registration of refugees is extremely weak and registration by sex is even weaker. As a result policies are not designed for the preponderance of women," stressing the picture was less clear in camps used by men as resting places for combat.

From the Centre, based at the medical faculty of Belgium's Catholic University of Louvain since 1973 and funded for some projects by the EU's emergency aid arm ECHO, she argues that a series of simple and cheap changes would make a world of difference.
REPRODUCING TO SURVIVE

"People think that if you are a refugee or in a camp you don't have sex and you don't have babies. Nothing can be further from the truth," said the plain-speaking professor, explaining one of the fallacies of aid policy.
In the televised images of dirty and diseased refugee camps the last thing that springs to mind is procreation. But for hungry and frightened refugees it is a way of survival.
"They are rapidly having babies because of a sense of being eliminated, a sense of dying off. They have a strong sense of survival of the species," Guha-Sapir said.

While the average birth rate in developed countries is 28 per 1000 people, it rises to 42 per 1000 in Ethiopia's roughest camp, with women usually having their first baby as early as 15 and each woman having four live or still-born children.
Suffering from stress, malnutrition, malaria or anaemia 12.6 percent and 24.8 percent have had abortions, either spontaneous or induced, in the Western Ethiopian camps of Bonga and Fugnido.
In Ethiopia the centre is developing a health strategy for aid agencies and examining ways of setting up groups of informed women who can be responsible for their own health care.
SMALL CHANGES CAN MAKE A BIG DIFFERENCE
"Recent analysis in Ethiopia shows there are a series of relatively low-cost interventions which would make a difference to the services that the women have," Guha-Sapir said.
"That would go a long way to giving the services more efficiency and making them much more palatable to the women."
It was the shortcomings of the international response to the famines in Ethiopia and Somalia in the late 1980s and early 1990s which prompted her to set out on her work.

Creating an ante-natal centre, for example, is not just a matter of building four walls and putting a tin roof on it, she says. Planting a couple of trees or a bench could make the difference between the pregnant women coming or staying away.
"They have to cluster round in the sun at 42 (degrees) in the shade for half an hour to an hour...waiting to be seen by the nurse. That does not encourage the women to come."
Many women will also stay away if they have to be seen by a male nurse or have a male translator on hand to talk about gynaecological problems.
Lack of education means three out of five women visit ante- natal centres after 20 weeks of pregnancy, instead of after 12.

While there is no need to send midwives and nurses to help with giving birth, a simple toolkit of a clean blade and piece of plastic to replace the strong grass used in some camps to tie umbilical cords could help avoid infection and ensure clean and safe birth, she says.
"This can be solved with a bit of imagination and a bit of creativity," said Guha-Sapir.
HIGH AWARENESS OF AIDS, LITTLE OF FAMILY PLANNING
"A very large number are aware of AIDS. We are talking about 80-90 percent. But barely 20 percent of the women have heard about family planning -- there's a very great room for improvement.

"They have flooded the camps with condoms. The supply of condoms is not a problem. But they have done nothing to increase the demand for the condoms," Guha-Sapir said, pointing to just another area where all that is lacking is a little thought.
